The bank's director argued that the figures justify the running cost of the colder store for accessions that are not duplicated elsewhere.
RW_M2H.why: The argument is that the colder store earns its running cost, which requires both figures set against each other to show the size of the difference. Reporting only the 31% at 4°C shows that some seed survives the warmer store and gives no measure of what the colder one adds.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Seed held at 4°C still showed 31% germination after twenty years.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The two storage temperatures tested differed by 24 degrees Celsius.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The bank tested only a single wheat accession over the twenty-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.content: After twenty years, 94% of seed held at −20°C germinated, against 31% of seed held at 4°C.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the team's conclusion?
RW_M2H.passage:
Cheeses lose mass in the cave, and how much they lose depends on the humidity they are held at. A team weighed batches of identical wheels held for ninety days at three humidities and recorded the mean loss.
Relative humidityMean mass lost in 90 days
80%11.4%
88%6.9%
95%3.1%
The team concluded that a maker who wants a thin rind and a moist paste should hold the cave near the top of this range.
RW_M2H.why: The conclusion recommends the humid end of the range, so the supporting datum has to be the one showing the smallest loss there and the contrast with the dry end. Citing the middle result alone reports a figure without connecting it to any recommendation about where to hold the cave.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Wheels at 88% humidity lost 6.9% of their mass, a figure between the other two results.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Wheels at 80% humidity lost 11.4% of their mass, the largest loss the team recorded.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The three humidities tested differed from one another by no more than fifteen percentage points.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Wheels at 95% humidity lost 3.1% of their mass, less than a third of the 11.4% lost at 80%.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the curer's argument?
RW_M2H.passage:
Water activity, rather than total moisture, sets the limit below which an organism cannot grow. A laboratory measured the lowest activity at which each of four organisms would multiply.
OrganismLowest water activity permitting growth
Clostridium botulinum0.94
Staphylococcus aureus0.86
Most yeasts0.80
Xerophilic moulds0.61
A curer who dries fish to a water activity of 0.83 argued that the product is safe from every organism on this list that causes acute illness, though not from spoilage.
RW_M2H.why: The claim is that the illness-causing organisms are excluded at 0.83 while spoilage organisms are not, which needs the two bacteria placed above that figure and the yeasts and moulds below it. Citing the mould's 0.61 alone establishes that spoilage remains possible but says nothing about the bacteria the curer claims to have excluded.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Clostridium botulinum requires 0.94, the highest activity recorded for any organism on the list.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The four organisms span a range of water activities from 0.61 to 0.94.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Both bacteria on the list require an activity above 0.83, while the yeasts and moulds do not.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Xerophilic moulds grow at 0.61, the lowest activity recorded for any organism on the list.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2H.passage: The hillside root cellars of Appalachia are almost always cut into a north-facing slope, and the reason is not that north-facing ground is colder in winter. In winter the door is shut and the earth around the chamber governs everything. It is in the shoulder seasons, when the door must be opened daily and the sun is low enough to reach into a doorway, that a south-facing entrance admits a wedge of direct light and a pulse of warm air with every visit. The orientation is therefore chosen to protect the store during _____
RW_M2H.why: The passage rules out winter, when the door stays shut, and points to the shoulder seasons of daily opening and a low sun as the vulnerable time. The option about summer is excluded by the passage's own detail that a high sun cannot reach into the doorway.

choices.label: A
choices.content: the periods when the cellar is opened rather than the coldest part of the year.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the winter months, when the surrounding earth is least able to insulate the chamber.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the hours of darkness, when the temperature outside falls furthest.

choices.label: D
choices.content: the summer, when the sun stands too high to enter a doorway at all.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2H.passage: The natural ice trade did not shrink gradually. Mechanical plants using compressed ammonia were producing ice in New Orleans by the 1870s at a price that pond ice could still undercut, and the harvesters were untroubled. What finished them was that a mechanical plant could be put up wherever ice was wanted, while a pond crop had to be cut in one place, held through a summer and carried hundreds of miles. Once the plants had multiplied, the harvester's price advantage applied to a product whose costs the buyer no longer had to bear at all. This suggests that the trade's collapse turned less on price than on _____
RW_M2H.why: The passage grants the harvesters a lasting price advantage and locates the decisive change in plants being built where the ice was wanted, which removes the storage and carriage the trade existed to perform. The option about costs rising too slowly contradicts the passage's statement that pond ice could still undercut the plants.

choices.label: A
choices.content: the disappearance of the distance that had made the harvesters' service necessary.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the failure of harvesters to reduce their costs as quickly as their competitors did.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the unwillingness of buyers to accept ice produced by an unfamiliar method.

choices.label: D
choices.content: a decline in the quality of the ice that ponds were able to yield.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: When Arthur DeVries drew blood from an Antarctic fish in the early 1960s and found that it resisted freezing far better than its salt content could _____ was looking at a class of molecule that nobody had proposed and that no existing theory of cold tolerance required.
RW_M2H.why: The long opening clause introduced by the subordinating conjunction must be closed with a comma before the main clause begins. A semicolon cannot follow a dependent clause, and omitting the mark leaves the reader to find the join unaided.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: Gutting a herring by hand takes a fraction of a second and removes only the gills and the long gut, leaving the pyloric caeca in _____ they carry the digestive enzymes that ripen the flesh during the weeks the fish spends in salt.
RW_M2H.why: Two independent statements meet here, and the semicolon separates them while the comma sets off the single word that comments on the first. Running them together with no mark at all leaves the second statement grafted onto the first without any boundary.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: The tool that did the real work on a frozen pond was not the saw but the ice _____ heavy toothed blade set in a wooden frame and dragged behind a horse, it cut a groove two thirds of the way through the sheet in a single pass.
RW_M2H.why: A complete sentence ends at the tool's name, and what follows is a second complete sentence beginning with the article that introduces the description. A comma between them joins two independent clauses without a conjunction.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: A logger left in a chamber a hundred metres from the entrance recorded temperatures over three years, and the spread between the highest and lowest readings across the whole period was _____ tenths of a degree.
RW_M2H.why: Nothing here interrupts the sentence: the measurement completes the predicate directly and takes no mark before it. Any punctuation after the number would separate a verb from its own complement.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: The floor of a well-built ice house slopes to a central drain, and the drain _____ through a water trap so that the melt can leave without letting warm air in behind it.
RW_M2H.why: The subject of the second clause is a single drain, so the verb takes the singular form. The plural form would agree with nothing in the sentence, and neither non-finite form supplies the clause with a main verb.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: Freezer burn is not burning and not really freezing either. Ice on the surface of a stored food passes straight to vapour without melting, and the dry, discoloured patch it _____ behind is what the name describes.
RW_M2H.why: The relative clause has the singular ice as its subject and needs a present-tense singular verb to match the sentence's other verbs. The past perfect form places the action before a past reference point that the sentence never establishes.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: Racks in a smokehouse are hung with a hand's width between them, since fish that touch one another leave pale patches where the smoke never reached _____ surfaces.
RW_M2H.why: The surfaces belong to the fish, which is plural in this sentence, so the plural possessive is required. The contraction is a subject and a verb and cannot modify a noun at all.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: Smoke reaches a fish as a suspension of droplets, and what settles on the skin depends on how wet that skin is. A fish taken straight from the brine carries a film of water that the droplets dissolve into and run off. _____ curers hang the fish for several hours first, until the surface has dried to the tacky, glossy layer they call the pellicle.
RW_M2H.why: The practice described is the response to the problem set out in the previous sentence, so the transition marks a consequence. A comparison marker would set the drying against something else in the passage, and nothing else is offered for it to be compared with.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: A wood frog begins converting liver glycogen to glucose within minutes of ice touching its skin, and the blood concentration can rise sixtyfold in eight hours. In a mammal a concentration of that order would be a medical emergency. _____ the frog clears it over several days after thawing with no lasting damage that anyone has been able to detect.
RW_M2H.why: The sentence sets the frog's harmless recovery against the emergency the same figure would represent in a mammal, so a contrastive transition is required. A consequence marker would make the harmless clearance follow from the emergency, which reverses the relation.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: The Romans drew salt at Droitwich from natural brine springs rather than from the sea, and the springs were strong enough to be boiled straight down without any preliminary concentration. Sea water at three per cent needs enormous quantities of fuel before it will yield anything. _____ an inland spring at twenty-five per cent could be worked profitably in a climate where a coastal saltern would never have dried a pond.
RW_M2H.why: The sentence sets the workable inland spring against the fuel-hungry sea water just described, so the transition marks an opposition. An example marker would present the spring as an instance of the sea-water difficulty rather than as its counterpart.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain how a low-cost device changed the sellers' commercial position, not merely the condition of the crop. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A trial in northern Nigeria stored aubergines in pot-in-pot coolers and in open baskets.
  • Aubergines in open baskets were unsaleable after three days.
  • Aubergines in the coolers remained saleable for twenty-seven days.
  • The coolers cost about two dollars each to make from local clay.
  • Sellers using the coolers could hold stock until prices rose instead of selling at once.
RW_M2H.why: The goal asks for the commercial change and not just the storage life, so the response has to carry the cost and the twenty-seven days through to the sellers' new freedom to wait for a better price. Giving the two storage lives reports the crop's condition and stops short of the commercial point the goal names.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The pot-in-pot coolers used in the trial cost about two dollars each to make from local clay.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A trial in northern Nigeria compared aubergines stored in pot-in-pot coolers with aubergines stored in open baskets.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Coolers costing about two dollars to make from local clay kept aubergines saleable for twenty-seven days against three days in open baskets, which let sellers hold their stock until prices rose rather than selling everything at once.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Aubergines held in pot-in-pot coolers remained saleable for twenty-seven days, while those in open baskets were unsaleable after three.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain what the comparison between the two groups shows about how the trait arose. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Antarctic fishes and several northern beetles both survive below the freezing point of their body fluids.
  • The fishes use glycoproteins built from a repeating sugar-bearing tripeptide.
  • The beetles use a protein with no sugar and an unrelated repeating structure.
  • Both molecules bind to the surface of a growing ice crystal and stop it enlarging.
  • The two lineages have been separate for hundreds of millions of years.
RW_M2H.why: The goal asks what the comparison shows about the trait's origin, so the response must set the unrelated structures against the shared function and the long separation, and draw the conclusion that the trait arose twice. Naming the two different molecules states the difference without saying what follows from it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Both molecules work by binding to the surface of a growing ice crystal and stopping it from enlarging.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Lineages separate for hundreds of millions of years arrived at molecules with nothing in common structurally, a sugar-bearing tripeptide in the fishes and a sugarless protein in the beetles, yet both bind to a growing ice crystal and stop it enlarging, so the trait was reached twice rather than inherited once.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Antarctic fishes and several northern beetles both survive below the freezing point of their body fluids.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The fishes use glycoproteins built from a repeating sugar-bearing tripeptide, while the beetles use a protein with no sugar at all.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain how an organism usually treated as a pest contributes to the finished cheese. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Mimolette is ripened with a mite, Acarus siro, living on its crust.
  • The mites graze the crust and leave it pitted and grey.
  • The pitting increases the crust's surface area many times over.
  • Air and moisture reach the paste more readily through a pitted crust than a smooth one.
  • Wheels kept free of mites ripen more slowly and taste flatter.
RW_M2H.why: The goal asks what the organism contributes, so the response must carry the pitting through to the enlarged surface, the readier exchange of air and moisture, and the poorer result without it. Reporting that the mites leave the crust pitted describes the damage and stops before the benefit the goal asks about.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Mimolette is ripened with a mite, Acarus siro, that lives on the crust of the wheel.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The mites graze the crust of the cheese and leave it pitted and grey rather than smooth.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Wheels kept free of mites ripen more slowly than wheels on which the mites are allowed to graze.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Grazing mites leave the crust pitted and grey, which multiplies its surface area so that air and moisture reach the paste far more readily than through a smooth crust, and wheels kept free of them ripen more slowly and taste flatter.

MATH_M1.stem: In one season a saltworks drew salt from seven pans. Six of the pans each gave the same mass of salt, and the seventh gave 140 kilograms less than each of the other six. The seven pans together gave 4,060 kilograms. How many kilograms of salt did each of the six equal pans give?
MATH_M1.check: Six pans of p kilograms and a seventh of p - 140 give 7p - 140 = 4,060, so 7p = 4,200 and p = 600.

MATH_M1.stem: An ice house is drawn on through the summer. Once 260 tonnes had been taken out of it, the mass still stored was three fifths of the mass that had been stored before any was taken out. How many tonnes were stored before any was taken out?

A saltworks watches two evaporating pans. The mass of salt drawn from the first, in kilograms, is 18d + 40 after d days of drying. The second pan gives 24 kilograms a day and already held 16 kilograms of salt when the drying began. After how many days of drying have the two pans given equal masses of salt?
MATH_M1.check: The second pan gives 24d + 16, and 18d + 40 = 24d + 16 leaves 6d = 24, so d = 4.

MATH_M1.stem: An ice house is drawn down at a steady rate through the summer. On the 8th day of the summer it held 186 tonnes of ice, and on the 26th day it held 132 tonnes. On which day of the summer does this rate leave the ice house empty?
MATH_M1.check: 54 tonnes go in 18 days, so 3 tonnes a day, and 186 - 3(d - 8) = 0 gives d = 70.

MATH_M1.stem: A saltworks pays 560 pounds in fixed costs for a season and a further 0.35 pound for every bushel of salt it draws, and it sells every bushel it draws for 2.40 pounds. What is the least number of bushels the works must draw and sell for the season's profit to be at least 900 pounds?
MATH_M1.check: 2.40b - (560 + 0.35b) is at least 900 once 2.05b is at least 1,460, so b is at least 712.19 and the least whole number of bushels is 713.

MATH_M1.stem: The mass of ice left in a store, in tonnes, is modelled by M = 310 - 4.6w, where w is the number of weeks since the store was closed. The store is emptied and swept as soon as no more than 15 percent of its original mass is left. After how many whole weeks is the store emptied and swept?
MATH_M1.check: 15 percent of 310 is 46.5, and 310 - 4.6w is at most 46.5 once w is at least 57.28, so the store is emptied in week 58.

MATH_M1.stem: An ice gang cuts blocks in two sizes: a large block has a mass of 42 kilograms and a small block a mass of 26 kilograms. In one day the gang cut 96 blocks with a combined mass of 3,232 kilograms. How many large blocks did the gang cut that day?
A saltworks estimates the tonnage it will draw from p pans as \((5p+6)(2p-3)\). Which expression is equivalent to this estimate?
MATH_M1.check: Multiplying out gives 10p squared minus 15p plus 12p minus 18, which is 10p squared minus 3p minus 18.

MATH_M1.stem: A packer's rule of thumb puts the number of ice blocks a chamber will take at \(\sqrt{72n^{5}}\), where n is a measure of the chamber and \(n>0\). Which expression is equivalent to this rule?
MATH_M1.check: 72 is 36 times 2 and n to the fifth is n to the fourth times n, so the square root is 6 n squared times the square root of 2n.

MATH_M1.stem: The sluice of a salt pan is set at a number x, and the setting must satisfy \((2x-7)^{2}=81\). What is the positive value of x that satisfies this equation?
MATH_M1.check: 2x - 7 is either 9 or -9, giving x = 8 or x = -1, and only 8 is positive.

MATH_M1.stem: The ice remaining in a store is modelled by \(T(w)=240\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{w}\) tonnes, where w is the number of weeks since the store was closed. According to this model, how many tonnes of ice are lost during the second week alone?
MATH_M1.check: The model gives 180 tonnes after one week and 135 after two, so the second week alone costs 45 tonnes.

MATH_M1.stem: The temperature inside an ice house, in degrees Celsius, h hours after its door is opened on a summer day is modelled by \(T(h)=11-8\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{h}\). As h increases without bound, the temperatures this model gives come closer and closer to what value, in degrees Celsius?
MATH_M1.check: One half raised to h falls towards 0 as h grows, so the subtracted term vanishes and the model approaches 11.

MATH_M1.stem: The number of blocks an ice gang cuts in one shift is modelled by \(B(s)=-s^{2}+22s-40\), where s is the number of sawyers in the gang. What is the greatest number of sawyers for which this model gives a positive number of blocks?
MATH_M1.check: The model is positive between the roots of s squared minus 22s plus 40, which are 2 and 20, so the greatest whole number of sawyers is 19.

MATH_M1.stem: Ice is cut into blocks measuring 0.5 metre by 0.4 metre by 0.3 metre, and this ice has a mass of 920 kilograms for each cubic metre. A sledge may carry a load of at most 1,150 kilograms. What is the greatest number of whole blocks the sledge may carry at once?
MATH_M1.check: A block is 0.06 cubic metre and so 55.2 kilograms, and 1,150 divided by 55.2 is 20.83, so 20 blocks may go on.

How much greater is the range of the Millpond readings than the range of the Nether Pond readings, in centimetres?
MATH_M1.check: The Millpond readings run from 13 to 21, a range of 8, and the Nether Pond readings from 16 to 18, a range of 2, so the difference is 6.

MATH_M1.stem: In one season a saltworks pumped 46,000 cubic metres of sea water into its pans and drew 1,472 tonnes of salt from them. Working at the same yield, how many cubic metres of sea water must the works pump to draw 1,840 tonnes of salt?
MATH_M1.check: 1,840 is 1.25 times 1,472, and 1.25 times 46,000 cubic metres is 57,500.

MATH_M1.stem: The floor of a root cellar is a rectangle measuring 4.5 metres by 3.2 metres. It is given an even layer of dry sand over the whole of its area, and 2.16 cubic metres of sand are used. What is the depth, in metres, of the layer of sand?
MATH_M1.check: The floor is 14.4 square metres, and 2.16 divided by 14.4 is 0.15.

MATH_M1.stem: An ice house has a square floor of side 16 metres. A straight partition runs from one corner of the floor to the middle point of a side that does not meet that corner. What is the length, in metres, of the partition?
MATH_M1.check: The partition is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 16 and 8, and the square root of 320 is 8 root 5.

MATH_M1.stem: A round salt pan has a radius of 12 metres, and a level walk of the same width all the way round is laid outside it. The walk covers \(52\pi\) square metres. What is the width, in metres, of the walk?
MATH_M1.check: The walk is the ring between circles of radius 12 + w and 12, so (12 + w) squared less 144 is 52, giving w squared + 24w - 52 = 0 and w = 2.

MATH_M1.stem: A wedge cut out of the ice by an ice saw is a right triangle ABC whose right angle is at C. The leg BC measures 8 metres and the triangle has an area of 60 square metres. What is the value of \(\tan A\)?
MATH_M1.check: Half of AC times 8 is 60, so AC is 15, and the tangent of A is BC over AC, or 8 over 15.

MATH_M2E.stem: The number of herring still hanging on a smokehouse rack h hours after the fire is lit is given by 340 - 12h. How many herring are still hanging 9 hours after the fire is lit?
MATH_M2E.check: 340 minus 12 times 9 is 340 minus 108, which is 232.

MATH_M2E.stem: A curer packs smoked herring 8 to a box. After packing as many full boxes as possible from 236 herring, 4 herring were left over. How many full boxes did the curer pack?
MATH_M2E.check: 236 less the 4 left over is 232, and 232 divided by 8 is 29.

MATH_M2E.stem: A cheese cave takes 9 wheels in each row on its shelves. How many rows does it take to hold 153 wheels, with every row filled?
MATH_M2E.check: 153 divided by 9 is 17.

MATH_M2E.stem: The mass of a cheese wheel, in kilograms, w weeks after it is carried into the cave is given by m = 4.6 - 0.05w. What is the mass of a wheel, in kilograms, 12 weeks after it is carried in?
MATH_M2E.check: 4.6 minus 0.05 times 12 is 4.6 minus 0.6, which is 4.0.

MATH_M2E.stem: The number of herring a smokehouse can hang is given by 6r + 24, where r is the number of extra rails fitted above the hearth. Which is the best interpretation of the 24 in this expression?
MATH_M2E.check: Setting r to 0 leaves 24, the number hung with no extra rail fitted.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The number of herring each extra rail lets the smokehouse hang

choices.label: C

MATH_M2E.stem: A curer hangs x strings of herring on one smoking rack. The rack is safely loaded whenever \(5x+8\le 43\). What is the greatest number of strings that leaves the rack safely loaded?
MATH_M2E.check: 5x is at most 35, so x is at most 7.

MATH_M2E.stem: A curer charges, in pence, 7f + 40 to smoke f fish for a customer. What does the curer charge, in pence, to smoke 22 fish?
MATH_M2E.check: 7 times 22 is 154, and 154 plus 40 is 194.

MATH_M2E.stem: A curer works out a load's rate figure as \(15p+35\). Which expression is equivalent to this figure?
MATH_M2E.check: 5 divides both 15p and 35, leaving 3p and 7.

MATH_M2E.stem: A cheese cave's air-change figure is written as \(\sqrt{81b^{4}}\), where \(b>0\). Which expression is equivalent to this figure?
MATH_M2E.check: The square root of 81 is 9 and the square root of b to the fourth is b squared.

MATH_M2E.stem: The number of days a cheese wheel needs in the cave is modelled by \(\frac{120}{x}\), where x is the number of degrees Celsius by which the cave stands above freezing. How many days does the model give when x is 8?
MATH_M2E.check: 120 divided by 8 is 15.

MATH_M2E.stem: A curer's smoke index x satisfies \(5^{x}=625\). What is the value of the smoke index?
MATH_M2E.check: 625 is 5 times 5 times 5 times 5, so x = 4.

MATH_M2E.stem: The number of minutes of smoking a curer allows at draught setting x is \(\frac{200}{x+3}\). How many minutes does this allow at draught setting 7?
MATH_M2E.check: 7 plus 3 is 10, and 200 divided by 10 is 20.

MATH_M2E.stem: A cheese cave's shelf plan uses the expression \(4y^{2}-36\). Which expression is equivalent to this?

MATH_M2E.stem: A shelf board for a cheese cave is a rectangle 120 centimetres long and 45 centimetres wide, with a square of side 15 centimetres cut out of one corner to clear a post. What is the area, in square centimetres, of the board?
MATH_M2E.check: 120 times 45 is 5,400, and 15 squared is 225, so 5,400 - 225 is 5,175.

MATH_M2E.stem: A smoke baffle is cut as a triangle whose three angles measure 3n°, 4n° and 5n°. What is the value of n?
MATH_M2E.check: The three angles add to 180, so 12n = 180 and n = 15.

MATH_M2E.stem: A smokehouse chimney is a hollow prism 7 metres tall whose inside cross-section is a square of side 0.9 metre. What is the volume, in cubic metres, of the space inside the chimney?
MATH_M2E.check: 0.9 squared is 0.81, and 0.81 times 7 is 5.67.

MATH_M2E.stem: A brace under a smokehouse rafter is cut as a triangle with one right angle and two sides of equal length. Each of the two equal sides measures 9 centimetres. What is the length, in centimetres, of the third side?
MATH_M2E.check: The two equal sides are the legs, so the third side is the square root of 81 + 81, which is 9 root 2.

MATH_M2H.stem: A curer's loading rule is the pair of equations \(ax+4y=26\) and \(3x-2y=5\), where a is a constant, x is the number of racks of herring and y the number of racks of mackerel. The pair has the solution in which \(x=3\). What is the value of a?
MATH_M2H.check: Putting x = 3 into 3x - 2y = 5 gives y = 2, and then 3a + 8 = 26 gives a = 6.

MATH_M2H.stem: A smokehouse fires n batches of fish one after another. Each batch takes t hours in the smoke, and the hearth must be left to cool for c hours between one batch and the next. Which expression gives the total number of hours from the moment the first batch goes in to the moment the last batch comes out?
MATH_M2H.check: There are n spells of smoking and only n - 1 gaps, since no cooling follows the last batch.

MATH_M2H.stem: A curer's two smoking ovens hold 348 fish between them. If 40 fish were moved from the larger oven to the smaller, the larger would still hold 26 more fish than the smaller. How many fish does the larger oven hold?
MATH_M2H.check: Moving 40 across changes the difference by 80, so the true difference is 106, and 348 plus 106 halved is 227.

MATH_M2H.stem: On a plan of a cheese cave a straight line passes through the points \((a,3a)\) and \((3a,11a)\), where a is a positive constant. The line crosses the vertical axis at the point \((0,b)\). What is the value of b in terms of a?
MATH_M2H.check: The slope is 8a over 2a, which is 4, and 3a = 4a + b gives b = -a.

MATH_M2H.stem: A cheese cave will accept a wheel only if its mass m, in kilograms, satisfies \(\left|m-38\right|\le 2.5\). Which of the following gives every acceptable mass?
MATH_M2H.check: The condition says m is within 2.5 of 38, which is every mass from 35.5 to 40.5.

MATH_M2H.stem: A cheese cave's shelf survey uses a line in the xy-plane whose equation is \(y=px+q\). The line passes through \((0,-5)\) and is parallel to the line through \((1,5)\) and \((4,17)\). What is the value of \(p+q\)?
MATH_M2H.check: The slope of the second line is 12 over 3, which is 4, and passing through (0, -5) makes q equal -5, so p + q is -1.

MATH_M2H.stem: A curer opens a smokehouse flue by x notches, and the draught is judged sufficient whenever \(\frac{5x-3}{4}\ge x+2\). For which numbers of notches is the draught judged sufficient?
MATH_M2H.check: Multiplying through by 4 gives 5x - 3 at least 4x + 8, which leaves x at least 11.

MATH_M2H.stem: An affineur's yield curve \(y=f(x)\) crosses the x-axis at \(x=-4\) and at \(x=6\). The function g is defined by \(g(x)=f(x+2)\). What is the greater of the two values of x at which the graph of \(y=g(x)\) crosses the x-axis?
MATH_M2H.check: g is 0 where x + 2 is -4 or 6, that is where x is -6 or 4, and the greater is 4.

MATH_M2H.stem: A curer's timing rule is written as \(x^{2}+14x+58\). Which expression is equivalent to this rule?
MATH_M2H.check: Half of 14 is 7, and 7 squared is 49, so the rule is (x + 7) squared plus 58 minus 49.

MATH_M2H.stem: An affineur's spacing rule uses the expression \(4x^{2}+kx+49\), where k is a positive constant, and this expression is the square of a binomial. What is the value of k?
MATH_M2H.check: The square of 2x plus 7 is 4x squared plus 28x plus 49, so k is 28.

MATH_M2H.stem: The number of wheels ripening in a cheese cave is modelled by \(R(t)=6\cdot 9^{\frac{t}{2}}\), where t is the number of months since the cave was filled. Which of the following is equivalent to \(R(t)\)?
MATH_M2H.check: 9 is 3 squared, so 9 raised to t over 2 is 3 raised to t.

MATH_M2H.stem: A curer's damper gauge reports a positive reading x for which \(x^{2}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}=23\). What is the value of \(x+\frac{1}{x}\)?
MATH_M2H.check: Squaring x plus its reciprocal gives 23 plus 2, which is 25, and the positive square root is 5.

MATH_M2H.stem: A smokehouse's output, in fish, is modelled by \(P(x)=-3x^{2}+42x-135\), where x is the number of hours the hearth is kept alight. The model gives an output of 0 at two values of x. What is the positive difference between those two values?
MATH_M2H.check: Dividing by -3 leaves x squared minus 14x plus 45, whose roots are 5 and 9.

MATH_M2H.stem: A cheese cave holds 45 wheels whose mean mass is 4.2 kilograms. A further w wheels, each of mass exactly 6 kilograms, are carried in, and the mean mass of all the wheels in the cave is then 4.5 kilograms. What is the value of w?
MATH_M2H.check: 189 plus 6w equals 4.5 times (45 + w), which leaves 1.5w equal to 13.5, so w = 9.

MATH_M2H.stem: A smokehouse working with 3 racks cures 45 fish an hour, and the number of fish cured in an hour varies directly with the number of racks in use. How many hours does the smokehouse take to cure 1,200 fish when 5 racks are in use?
MATH_M2H.check: Each rack cures 15 fish an hour, so 5 racks cure 75 an hour, and 1,200 divided by 75 is 16.

MATH_M2H.stem: A cheese cave holds Tomme wheels and Beaufort wheels in the ratio 5 to 3. After 48 more Beaufort wheels are carried in, the two kinds stand in the ratio 5 to 4. How many Tomme wheels are in the cave?
MATH_M2H.check: With 5k Tomme and 3k Beaufort, 4(5k) = 5(3k + 48) gives k = 48, so there are 240 Tomme wheels.

MATH_M2H.stem: A smokehouse hood is a cone with no base, open to the room below. Its rim is a circle of radius 60 centimetres, and the slanting sheet metal runs 100 centimetres from the rim to the point at the top. What is the area, in square centimetres, of the sheet metal in the hood?
MATH_M2H.check: The curved surface of a cone is pi times radius times slant height, which is 60 times 100 times pi.

MATH_M2H.stem: On a plan, a smoke baffle is a triangle with vertices at \((0,0)\), \((12,0)\) and \((12,5)\), and one unit on the plan stands for one centimetre. A second baffle is similar to the first, and the longest side of the second baffle is 39 centimetres. What is the area, in square centimetres, of the second baffle?
MATH_M2H.check: The first baffle has legs 12 and 5 and so a hypotenuse of 13 and an area of 30, the similarity ratio is 3, and area scales by 9.

MATH_M2H.stem: A smoking chamber is a rectangular room 12 metres long, 7 metres wide and 3 metres high. Four brick piers stand in it, each running from the floor to the ceiling and each 0.5 metre by 0.5 metre in cross-section. What is the volume, in cubic metres, of the space left inside the chamber?
MATH_M2H.check: The room is 252 cubic metres and each pier takes 0.75 cubic metre, so four piers take 3.

MATH_M2H.stem: A cheese cave's corner brace is a triangle with vertices A, B and C, and its one right angle stands at C. In the brace \(\cos A=\frac{20}{29}\) and the side AB measures 87 centimetres. What is the perimeter, in centimetres, of the brace?
MATH_M2H.check: AC is 20 over 29 of 87, which is 60, and BC is the square root of 7,569 - 3,600, which is 63, so the perimeter is 87 + 60 + 63.
